items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph:
Now that we understand the importance of overcommunicating, the next step is understanding how to effectively communicate.

“By communicate effectively, what I mean is, how can you best command the attention of those you are speaking to?” Pat once said. “Should you employ high decibels or low? Are you talking to your boss or your employee? Would a touch of humor help? Decide what you are trying to accomplish, whether you are trying to motivate, elicit a confession, ask for a raise, or instill confidence. Be clear on what you want to say, and say it in a way that is appropriate to your surroundings. Circumstances dictate how you need to speak. You don't holler at a golf tournament. And you don't whisper at a forest fire.”

items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph: Pat believed there are three key components to effective personal communication:
Tone
Situation
Nonverbal Communication

items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph: We’ll discuss all three a little more in the next lesson.

items.name: — Pat Summitt
items.paragraph: I wouldn’t speak to a player in my office the same way I would on the court. Circumstances dictate how you need to speak, or whether you need to just shut up and listen. You don’t holler at a golf tournament. You don’t whisper in a forest fire.”

items.title: CONTINUE
items.completeHint: Complete the content above before moving on.

items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph: Pat was famous for her authoritative presence on the sidelines but would be the first to clarify that it wasn’t the only communication style she employed as a leader.

“I employ three completely different modes of communication as a coach,” she once said. “Off the court, I am a confidante and substitute mother. In that situation, my chief role is to listen, advise and comfort. In practice, I speak as a teacher who sometimes needs to employ severe methods in order to maintain the attention of the students.”

“In a game, I issue blunt commands and motivate our players to endure adverse situations. It’s a competitive situation with no time for politeness or misunderstanding. My different tones, taken out of context, would be counterproductive or even downright offensive in any other situation.”

items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph:
In the video we just watched, we went over four types of inflection and pitch and how each communicates a different sentiment when used properly:

Please click each to complete this element.

items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph: Knowing how and when to use different tones appropriately can be the difference between coming off as authoritative or weak, sensitive or insensitive, excited, or unenthusiastic.

items.completeHint: Complete the content above before moving on.

items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph:
The second component of personal communication is being able to appropriately assess each unique situation to determine the right level of communication.

“Frequently, knowing what to say to someone is all about time and location,” Pat once said. “You don’t always make the right call. There’s a judgment involved. You have to ask yourself, ‘What does this person need today?’ And you have to watch his or her body language.”
(Download the transcript below)

items.date: Here are a few elements to consider when it comes to situational communication:
items.title: Context of the Communication
items.description: Understanding the context of a conversation includes not only the physical setting but also the emotional backdrop of the communication.

items.title: Knowing Your Audience
items.description: Audience awareness is at the heart of situational communication. Different audiences require different approaches, vocabulary, and levels of formality.

items.title: Timing of the Communication
items.description: Timing can significantly influence communication effectiveness. Not every moment is ideal for every type of message; situational communicators recognize when to wait and when to act.

items.title: Nonverbal Communication
items.description: Body language, eye contact, posture, gestures and facial expressions—plays an equally important role in situational communication. Research shows that a large portion of human communication is non-verbal, meaning that words alone do not fully capture the message being conveyed. The non-verbal cues of the receiver can also help you gauge how your communication is being received. Are they sitting with their arms crossed? Scowling? etc.

items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph:
The point is, context can significantly affect how a message is received.

We’ll go over this more in the upcoming lesson.

items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph:
Pat once told a story of how the 1977 team had stayed up late one night drinking and partying until 4 a.m. in violation of team policies. When they showed up for practice the next day completely hungover, she debated how to respond. She considered giving them a tongue lashing but thought the better of it. Instead, she put trash cans on the baseline at the corners of the gym and conducted practice for four hours, by the end of which almost every player had vomited into one of the trash cans.

Her point was made.

“If all you ever do is yell, then you will be heard less and less,” she said. “That’s why sometimes, saying nothing at all can be just as powerful.”

One of Pat’s famous mannerisms is the “Summitt Stare” — a famous glare she often employed on the sidelines. The stare is said to have been so intense that it could make players and officials alike feel nervous or unsettled. Players and opponents knew that when they saw the stare, they were in for a tough game.

As a coach, Pat knew when to speak and when to be silent. The habit of communicating through body language is one that the best communicators have intentionally worked on over time, choosing which postures, attitude, or gestures to use in which situation so they convey their message in the most effective way.

items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph: Finally, all three of these communication principles — tone, situation, and nonverbal communication — take lifelong practice. Your skills will evolve as you do in your role, and new situations will constantly present themselves. You never reach the finish line of perfect communication, but with a little awareness and intentionality, you can make sure you’re prepared to communicate wisely and effectively in any situation.
